milestones.title: a sandbox with a whitelist and a fuel budget
milestones.task: Write validate(src) (return the parsed ast.Module or raise Rejected with a reason), instrument(tree) (return a new tree with ticks and float constants) and compile_restricted(src, fuel) (validate, instrument, compile, exec in a namespace that holds only abs, min, max and the fuel's tick under the name _tick, and return the priority function).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks that the seed, first fit and a fourteen-line program with while, if expressions, and and // are accepted; that all forty-two attack programs are rejected (imports, attribute escapes, open, eval, lambdas, comprehensions, **, strings, nested functions, the hidden _tick, a 1,500-deep nest of minus signs, a null byte, sources that are too long or have too many nodes); that instrument leaves its argument untouched and puts exactly one tick in the function and one per loop body; that instrumented code gives the same answers as plain Python; that fuel.used is exactly 4 after one call of a program with a three-turn loop; and that three non-terminating loops (while True, a counter that never reaches its limit, and an integer-squaring loop) all end in OutOfFuel with fuel.used equal to the budget plus one.
milestones.explain:
Everything in this lab runs code that nobody has read: the candidates are text produced by a mutation operator, and in a real system, by a model. Chapter 9 gave the evaluator a separate process and a two-second timer, and said honestly that this is isolation of mistakes, not a security boundary. This milestone takes the complementary approach, which works because the language is tiny: do not run what you have not read. Candidates may only use a handful of syntax constructs, and everything else is refused before a single line executes.

If ast, compile and exec are new to you, read Programs as Data (A0 chapter 21) first: it builds every tool this milestone uses, slowly. What follows is a recap. The tool is Python's own parser. ast.parse(src) turns source into a tree of nodes (Assign, BinOp, Name, Call, Import, Attribute, and so on), and a whitelist says which node types are allowed; anything not on the list is rejected. The alternative, a blacklist of dangerous things, always misses one. The classic example is ().__class__.__bases__[0], which reaches the base object class and from there every class in the interpreter without a single import or call to a function called anything dangerous. With a whitelist there is no need to think of it: Attribute and Subscript are simply not on the list. The given constant ALLOWED_NODES lists the permitted nodes (arithmetic, comparisons, if, while, assignments, abs/min/max calls); your validate adds the rules a type list cannot express: the function must be exactly def priority(item, rem):, calls may only name abs, min or max, names must exist, no name may begin with an underscore, constants must be small numbers, and the source must be short.

Why allow while at all, if the packing heuristic never needs a loop? Because a safe design does not rely on any one layer. The whitelist keeps out the dangerous; fuel bounds what is left. A step budget counts operations, not seconds, and it matters for two reasons. A wall-clock limit is nondeterministic: the same candidate passes on a fast machine and times out on a slow one, so an evolutionary run stops being reproducible, which is the property that makes it debuggable. And checking a clock inside interpreted code means either a separate process (slow to start, hundreds of thousands of times in a long run) or tracing every line.

The cheaper trick is to instrument the tree before compiling it: insert a call _tick() as the first statement of the function and as the first statement of every while body. A shared Fuel object counts the ticks and raises OutOfFuel when the budget is gone. Code that never loops costs one tick per call; code that loops forever eats the budget a tick per turn. The instrumented version of a small loop, produced by the lab's own code, shows the idea:

import ast
import solution as lab          # use `starter as lab` while you work

attacks = {
    "import":      "def priority(item, rem):\n    import os\n    return 1\n",
    "attribute":   "def priority(item, rem):\n    return (1).__class__\n",
    "open":        "def priority(item, rem):\n    return open('x')\n",
    "power":       "def priority(item, rem):\n    return item ** rem\n",
    "string":      "def priority(item, rem):\n    return 'tight'\n",
    "best fit":    lab.SEED_SRC,
}
for name, src in attacks.items():
    try:
        lab.validate(src)
        print(f"{name:10s} accepted")
    except lab.Rejected as e:
        print(f"{name:10s} rejected: {e}")

loop = "def priority(item, rem):\n    i = 0\n    while i < 5:\n        i += 1\n    return i\n"
print(ast.unparse(lab.instrument(lab.validate(loop))))
for name, body in {"counter": loop,
                   "forever": "def priority(item, rem):\n    while True:\n        pass\n    return 1\n",
                   "squaring": "def priority(item, rem):\n    x = 9\n    while x > 0:\n        x = x * x\n    return x\n"}.items():
    fuel = lab.Fuel(1000)
    f = lab.compile_restricted(body, fuel)
    try:
        print(f"{name:9s} returned {f(40.0, 70.0)} after {fuel.used} ticks")
    except lab.OutOfFuel as e:
        print(f"{name:9s} OutOfFuel ({e}) after {fuel.used} ticks")
import     rejected: Import is not allowed
attribute  rejected: Attribute is not allowed
open       rejected: only abs, min and max may be called, with positional arguments
power      rejected: Pow is not allowed
string     rejected: constant 'tight' is not allowed
best fit   accepted
def priority(item, rem):
    _tick()
    i = 0.0
    while i < 5.0:
        _tick()
        i += 1.0
    return i
counter   returned 5.0 after 6 ticks
forever   OutOfFuel (more than 1000 steps) after 1001 ticks
squaring  OutOfFuel (more than 1000 steps) after 1001 ticks

Three details in that output are worth stopping on. The _tick() calls are invisible to the candidate's author, and the whitelist forbids any name that begins with an underscore, so a candidate cannot call, replace or silence the counter. The integer constants have all become floats (0.0, 5.0), which looks fussy and is the answer to the last case in the output: Python integers have no upper limit, so x = x * x in a loop squares an integer whose size doubles every turn, and a thousand turns would try to build a number with more digits than there are atoms in the universe, long before the fuel counter was consulted. Floats overflow to infinity instead, which is harmless (and caught later, in milestone 2). Finally, the rejection lines at the top of the output show the kind of message the evaluator will carry: not "something went wrong" but which rule was broken.

Common misconception

"A whitelist sandbox makes it safe to run model-written code." It makes it safe to run model-written code in this tiny language, against a model that is mistaken or an operator that is random. Python's real standard library is a very different surface, and a whitelist over it would be a research project. For anything an adversary can reach, the answer is still an operating-system boundary: a container or virtual machine with no credentials and no network, as in sandboxes and permissions and the untrusted-code design of the online code judge studio. This milestone teaches the first layer of defence, the one that costs nothing per candidate, not a replacement for the second.

milestones.title: an evaluator that never raises
milestones.task: Write pack(items, priority) (return the number of bins) and evaluate(src, instances, fuel_budget=FUEL) (return an Outcome, never raise). Create one Fuel for the whole call. Wrap the compiled function in a checker that converts the arguments to floats and validates the return value; catch Rejected, OutOfFuel, the checker's complaint and every other exception separately, in that order of specificity.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks pack by hand (60+40 and 50+50 make two bins; best fit packs [60, 70, 30, 40] into 2 bins and first fit needs 3; the priority function is asked only about bins the item fits in; ties go to the earliest bin) and against an independent packer on eight seeded instances with five different priority functions; that best fit scores 130.3 and first fit 130.7 bins on the ten training instances; that steps equals the number of priority calls and that a budget one step short is a timeout (so the budget really is shared); twelve misbehaving programs, each with its expected status; and that six junk strings, including a null byte and an emoji, produce rejected outcomes instead of exceptions.
milestones.explain:
An evaluation is a function from a program (text) to a result, and the main design rule from chapter 9 is that it must be total: every possible input maps to some result, and nothing a candidate does can escape as an exception into the controller, because an unhandled error would lose hours of search. So the result is not a number but an Outcome with a status and a score that exists only when the status is ok:

StatusMeaningExample
rejectedThe sandbox refused it. It never ran.an import, a string constant, a syntax error
errorIt ran and raised.division by zero, a name read before it was assigned
timeoutIt ran out of fuel.while True, or a loop of 2,000 turns on every call
bad_valueIt returned something that is not a finite number.a boolean, None, infinity, nan
okIt packed all the instances.mean bins = 130.3

The bad_value row is the lesson of chapter 9's wrong-type candidate, which returned the string 'tight' for every bin: Python compares equal strings happily, no bin ever has a strictly higher priority, the packing degenerates to first fit, and the evaluator reported a respectable, meaningless 130.2. Here a string constant is rejected statically, but the same hole reappears through every other path: return item < rem yields a boolean, which is also a number in Python (True > False), and an expression that overflows gives infinity, and infinity minus infinity gives nan, which compares false against everything and corrupts the "highest priority" test silently. Check the value on every call, and accept only a finite int or float (type(v) in (int, float), which excludes bool).

Two more pieces. pack is the packing loop of chapter 9: for each item, ask priority(item, rem) of every feasible bin (rem >= item), take the highest, and break ties toward the earliest bin; open a new bin if none fits. And the fuel budget is shared by all the instances of one evaluation, so that a program that takes 2,000 steps per call is a timeout even though no single call looks long, which is what stops a slow-but-finite candidate from eating a whole search. The evaluator also records the number of bins used on each instance, a tuple that the next milestones call the program's signature.

The script below evaluates seven programs, two good and five that misbehave. The numbers are real: best fit and first fit reproduce chapter 9's 130.3 and 130.7 bins, and the "steps" column is the number of times priority was called.

import solution as lab          # use `starter as lab` while you work

train = lab.make_instances(lab.TRAIN_SEEDS)          # 10 instances of 300 items, as in chapter 9
many = " * ".join(["1000000000"] * 40)               # overflows a float to infinity
cases = {
    "best fit":       lab.SEED_SRC,
    "first fit":      lab.FIRST_FIT_SRC,
    "divide by zero": "def priority(item, rem):\n    return -(rem - item) / (item - item)\n",
    "forever":        "def priority(item, rem):\n    while True:\n        pass\n    return 1\n",
    "a boolean":      "def priority(item, rem):\n    return item < rem\n",
    "infinity":       f"def priority(item, rem):\n    return {many}\n",
    "an import":      "def priority(item, rem):\n    import os\n    return 1\n",
}
for name, src in cases.items():
    out = lab.evaluate(src, train)
    print(f"{name:15s} {out.status:10s} score {out.score:7.2f}  steps {out.steps:6d}  {out.detail[:40]}")
best fit        ok         score  130.30  steps   2658  
first fit       ok         score  130.70  steps   2775  
divide by zero  error      score     inf  steps      1  ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
forever         timeout    score     inf  steps 400001  more than 400000 steps
a boolean       bad_value  score     inf  steps      1  priority returned True
infinity        bad_value  score     inf  steps      1  priority returned inf
an import       rejected   score     inf  steps      0  Import is not allowed

The infinite loop used 400,001 steps: one more than the budget, which is when Fuel raises. Notice also that divide by zero and a boolean stopped after a single step, on the very first call: an evaluator that fails fast on a broken candidate is a cheap one, and the controller can afford to feed it thousands.

milestones.title: a mutation operator on the syntax tree
milestones.task: Write edit_constant(tree, rng), edit_operator(tree, rng) and mutate(src, rng, attempts=10). In edit_constant use one rng.choice to pick the constant and one to pick the nudge; mutate must read the module-level tuple EDITS at call time (the check replaces it to test your fallback).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Over 200 seeds, edit_constant changes exactly one constant by -2, -1, +1 or +2, hits every constant and every nudge, never goes below zero and leaves the tree unchanged when there are none; edit_operator changes exactly one operator within its family, touches both families, and leaves ==, % and unary minus alone; mutate returns canonical, valid, deterministic children, at least 97% different from the parent, with at least 60 different children out of 150 seeds; it falls back to the parent when every edit corrupts or does nothing; and 300 tree edits of a 14-line program are all valid. Finally, a plain hill climber (keep a child if it is no worse) using your mutate for 500 steps must beat best fit by 0.4 bins on average over three seeds, and must climb further than the same hill climber using character flips.
milestones.explain:
Chapter 9 explained why a language model makes a good mutation operator: random edits to program text are almost always broken, and the model's edits mostly are not. The same is true of the stand-in, and for the same reason it needs to work on structure rather than characters. If you flip a random character of a ten-line program, you usually get a syntax error, or a name that does not exist, or a number glued to a letter. The script below compares the two on the seed program: 300 edits of each kind, counting the children that pass validate.

import random
import solution as lab          # use `starter as lab` while you work

seed = lab.canonical(lab.SEED_SRC)
rng = random.Random(7)
for i in range(4):
    print(f"--- child {i}")
    print(lab.mutate(seed, rng))

def flip(src, rng):                                   # an edit of the TEXT: replace one character
    i = rng.randrange(len(src))
    return src[:i] + rng.choice("0123456789+-*<>=() abcdefg\n") + src[i + 1:]

rng = random.Random(0)
print("valid children out of 300, tree edits:  ", sum(lab.is_valid(lab.mutate(seed, rng)) for _ in range(300)))
print("valid children out of 300, text flips:  ", sum(lab.is_valid(flip(seed, rng)) for _ in range(300)))
--- child 0
def priority(item, rem):
    gap = rem - item
    if gap >= 4:
        return -gap - 50
    return -gap
--- child 1
def priority(item, rem):
    gap = gap - item
    return -gap
--- child 2
def priority(item, rem):
    gap = rem + item
    return -gap
--- child 3
def priority(item, rem):
    gap = rem - item
    return --gap
valid children out of 300, tree edits:   300
valid children out of 300, text flips:   6

Tree edits give 300 valid children out of 300; character flips give 6. The tree operator is not cleverer than the text one, it is closed: it can only produce trees that are made of legal nodes, so unparsing a child always gives legal text. (ast.unparse also gives each tree one canonical spelling, which is why two programs that differ only in spacing are the same string and the loop can spot duplicates by comparing text.) Look at the four children: a new comparison inserted as a rule, an operator swapped from - to +, a doubled minus sign, and a name replaced by another.

The operator works the way a transformation of a tree should. Pick a node of a particular kind at random, change one thing about it, and unparse. The edits live in a small grammar of edits. Two of them you write, because they show the technique at its simplest; the rest are given, and you will use them through mutate:

EditWhat it does to the treeWho writes it
edit_constantNudge one number by -2, -1, +1 or +2 (never below 0).you
edit_operatorSwap one + - * or one < <= > >= for another of its family.you
edit_insert_ruleInsert if name cmp (name or number): return payoff after the leading assignments.given
edit_shapeWrap one expression of a return in abs, a negation, a shift, a %, min or max.given
edit_replace_nameReplace a name that is read by another name in scope.given
edit_deleteDelete one statement of the body, never the last.given

An edit takes (tree, rng), changes the tree in place, and returns True if it had something to edit or False if not (a program with no constants has nothing for edit_constant, and the seed is such a program). mutate(src, rng) chooses one edit from the tuple EDITS, applies it to a freshly parsed tree, and unparses. It then checks the child: it must differ from the parent and must pass is_valid. If not, mutate tries again, up to ten times, and as a last resort returns the parent unchanged. The check matters, because some given edits can produce a tree the sandbox refuses (edit_delete can remove the only assignment of a name that is still read), and because an edit that "succeeds" but changes nothing, like nudging a 0 down by one, would waste an evaluation.

Common misconception

"If the mutation operator only produces valid programs, the evaluator's error handling is redundant." Valid means the sandbox accepted the tree; it does not mean the program runs. Child 1 in the output above is gap = gap - item: every name in it exists somewhere in the function, so validate accepts it, and on its first call Python raises UnboundLocalError because gap is read before it is assigned. In the 500-call searches at the end of this lab, between 5 and 13 of every 450-odd evaluated programs end as error for exactly this kind of reason (or a modulus nudged down to zero). A real language model fails far more often, in far more creative ways. The sandbox and the evaluator are the net; the operator only decides how often the net is needed.

milestones.title: an island of clusters
milestones.task: Write softmax_weights(values, temperature), Island.add(src, outcome) and Island.sample(rng, k=2, cluster_temp=0.5, length_temp=50.0). add stores only ok outcomes in the cluster named by outcome.bins, keeps each cluster to the MAX_PER_CLUSTER shortest distinct programs (ties by text), and when the island has more than max_clusters clusters, drops the one with the lowest fitness (the earliest created if tied).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks the softmax by hand ([0, ln 3] gives [0.25, 0.75]; a temperature of 0.5 doubles the gap; values near -1000 do not underflow; extreme temperatures give a one-hot and a uniform distribution), then add (failed outcomes ignored, equal signatures share a cluster, duplicates ignored, the four-program cap, eviction of the lowest-fitness cluster and the tie rule), then sample with 4,000 draws per setting against the exact probabilities at three temperatures, the length preference inside a cluster, and the contract (1 to k distinct programs, worst cluster first, deterministic given the rng). The last test builds an island from four real programs and expects three clusters.
milestones.explain:
If every prompt contained the single best program, the database would collapse onto one family of solutions and the search would stall; chapter 9 described FunSearch's remedy. Programs are grouped by what they do, not by how they look. A cluster is the set of programs with the same signature, here the tuple of bin counts on the ten training instances. -(rem - item) and gap = rem - item; return -gap are different text and the same behaviour, so they share a cluster; changing any decision that changes any packing moves a program to a different one. Programs in a cluster are interchangeable as far as the score goes, so the database keeps the shortest few (at most four), which fights bloat.

The script builds one island from four programs. The numbers are real, and show the two spellings of best fit landing together.

import solution as lab          # use `starter as lab` while you work

train = lab.make_instances(lab.TRAIN_SEEDS)
programs = {
    "first fit":        lab.FIRST_FIT_SRC,
    "best fit":         lab.SEED_SRC,
    "best fit, spelt differently": "def priority(item, rem):\n    return -(rem - item)\n",
    "dead-gap rule":    "def priority(item, rem):\n    gap = rem - item\n    if gap == 0:\n        return 1000\n    if gap < 20:\n        return -gap - 50\n    return -abs(gap - 26)\n",
}
isl = lab.Island()
for name, src in programs.items():
    out = lab.evaluate(src, train)
    isl.add(lab.canonical(src), out)
    print(f"{name:28s} {out.score:7.2f} bins   signature starts {out.bins[:3]}")
print(len(isl), "programs in", len(isl.clusters), "clusters")
for sig, c in isl.clusters.items():
    print(f"  cluster {sig[:3]}... fitness {c['fitness']:.2f}, {len(c['programs'])} program(s), shortest {len(c['programs'][0])} characters")
first fit                     130.70 bins   signature starts (128, 133, 128)
best fit                      130.30 bins   signature starts (129, 131, 128)
best fit, spelt differently   130.30 bins   signature starts (129, 131, 128)
dead-gap rule                 128.40 bins   signature starts (126, 129, 125)
4 programs in 3 clusters
  cluster (128, 133, 128)... fitness -130.70, 1 program(s), shortest 37 characters
  cluster (129, 131, 128)... fitness -130.30, 2 program(s), shortest 49 characters
  cluster (126, 129, 125)... fitness -128.40, 1 program(s), shortest 150 characters

Choosing parents is a two-stage draw. First pick a cluster, with probability proportional to exp(fitness / Tc): a softmax over cluster fitness, where the temperature Tc (here 0.5 bins) sets how strongly high scorers are favoured. Then pick a program within the cluster by a softmax over minus its length, with its own temperature (50 characters here), so shorter programs are more likely. Draw this k times to fill the prompt, drop duplicates, and sort from worst cluster to best, so the best program is last, where a model's attention would look for "the next version".

The temperature is worth getting a feel for. With three clusters at fitness -130, -129 and -128:

TemperatureP(worst)P(middle)P(best)Behaviour
0.50.0160.1170.867mostly the best, sometimes the others
1.00.0900.2450.665gentler
10000.3330.3330.333uniform: fitness is ignored

(These are exp(f/T) normalised, which you can check with a calculator, and which the check verifies with 4,000 draws each.) Notice the scale: temperatures here are in bins because fitness is minus mean bins. That is why the best temperature is a property of the problem's score range, and why frameworks normalise the scores first.

One implementation trap: exp(-130 / 0.5) underflows to exactly zero in floating point, and so would every other term. The standard fix, subtracting the maximum before exponentiating, leaves the probabilities unchanged and keeps the largest term at exp(0) = 1. The check feeds your function values around -1000 to make sure you do.

milestones.title: islands, and replacing the weakest
milestones.task: Write Database.best() (the best program on any island with its fitness; ties go to the lowest island index) and Database.reseed(rng) (replace the weakest len // 2 islands as above and return the list of (replaced_index, source_index) pairs, weakest rank last).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It builds six islands with known best scores and expects islands 2, 4 and 0 (in rank order) to be replaced by copies of the best of islands 5, 3 or 1, with the survivors' contents untouched; checks 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 islands for how many are replaced; checks that a fresh database replaces the last half; that the same seed gives the same moves; that over 60 seeds every survivor is a source at least once; and finally runs 120 real steps and checks that a reseed never loses the best program.
milestones.explain:
One island with a cluster-based sampler still has a failure mode: if one family of ideas takes an early lead, the temperature keeps feeding it, and the others never get the evaluations they need to mature. FunSearch's second defence is to run several islands, independent sub-populations that never see each other's programs, so a family that dominates one island cannot crowd out the others. The loop gives each island its turn in rotation. OpenEvolve, in chapter 10, does the same with a ring and a migration_interval.

Independence has a cost: an island that has found nothing keeps spending calls on nothing. So every so often the database performs a reseed: rank the islands by the fitness of their best program, throw away the weakest half, and replace each discarded island with a fresh one that holds only the best program of a surviving island, chosen at random among the survivors. Effort drifts towards what works without ever collapsing to one lineage, because the replaced islands start with one program and grow their own clusters from it.

Three details define the rule exactly, and the check tests each. The ranking breaks ties by lower index, so a fresh database (every island holding the seed) always replaces the last half. With an odd number of islands, len // 2 are replaced (two of five), so the survivors are always the larger half. And the best program in the whole database must survive a reseed, since survivors are never touched. The given Island.fresh_from_best() builds the one-program island for you.

milestones.title: the loop, and an honest report
milestones.task: Write funsearch(budget, seed, ...) and report(src, train_seeds, test_seeds). One random.Random(seed) drives the whole run. Evaluate canonical(SEED_SRC) first (it does not count as a call), put it on every island, and keep a set of source texts already seen.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks the bookkeeping of short runs on two seeds (calls, trace, evaluations and status counts, determinism, validity of best_src), that parents arrive worst-first and the first call sees only the seed, the three bad mutators, that islands take turns and that reseed runs after calls 10, 20 and 30, report on best fit and first fit (130.77 held-out bins, lower bound 120.24), and then three real 500-call searches: each must save at least 1.2 bins on the training set and at least 0.7 on the held-out instances. A last search on two instances must look better on those two than on the held-out thirty.
milestones.explain:
Now the loop. The budget is counted in calls of the mutation operator, because with a real model that is the quantity that costs money and wall-clock time: ShinkaEvolve's paper is about needing far fewer of them than systems that, in its authors' words, need thousands of samples. Each call, in order: pick the island whose turn it is (call i works on island i % n_islands), draw k parents from it, ask the mutator for a child, skip the evaluation if that exact text has been seen before (a call that produced a duplicate is still a call, and still spent), otherwise evaluate it and store the result. After every reseed_every calls, reseed. Record the best fitness after every call, so you can plot the progress curve.

Evaluations are cheaper than calls here (a few milliseconds each), so the loop is fast. The things the check looks for are bookkeeping: that exactly budget calls are made, the trace never goes down, evaluations equals the sum of the status counts, the same seed reproduces the whole run, and three deliberately bad mutators cannot break anything. One returns its parent (no new program is ever evaluated), one returns garbage with an import in it (every child is rejected), and one returns infinite loops (every child is a timeout, paid for in fuel and nothing else).

The second function, report, is short and is the point of the lab. It takes a program and returns its mean bins on the training instances (the ten the search looked at) and on thirty held-out instances (seeds 100 to 129) that it never did, next to best fit's, and the saving on each. Chapter 16 spends a whole chapter on why this matters; the script below shows it happening.

import solution as lab          # use `starter as lab` while you work

def show(label, **kw):
    r = lab.funsearch(**kw)
    rp = lab.report(r.best_src, train_seeds=kw.get("train_seeds", lab.TRAIN_SEEDS))
    print(f"{label:34s} {r.evaluations:4d} programs  train {rp['train']:6.2f}  held-out {rp['test']:6.2f}   "
          f"saves {rp['gain_train']:.2f} / {rp['gain_test']:.2f}")
    return r

print(f"best fit: train 130.30, held-out 130.77; lower bound on the held-out instances {lab.report(lab.SEED_SRC)['lower_test']:.2f}")
for s in (1, 2, 3):
    show(f"500 calls, seed {s}", budget=500, seed=s)
show("3000 calls, seed 1", budget=3000, seed=1)
show("500 calls, searched on 2 instances", budget=500, seed=1, train_seeds=(0, 1))
r = lab.funsearch(500, 3)
print("\ncall:", *[(i + 1) for i in (0, 49, 99, 199, 299, 499)])
print("best bins so far:", *[f"{-r.trace[i]:.2f}" for i in (0, 49, 99, 199, 299, 499)])
print("\n" + r.best_src)
best fit: train 130.30, held-out 130.77; lower bound on the held-out instances 120.24
500 calls, seed 1                   458 programs  train 128.70  held-out 129.63   saves 1.60 / 1.13
500 calls, seed 2                   438 programs  train 128.80  held-out 129.57   saves 1.50 / 1.20
500 calls, seed 3                   467 programs  train 128.60  held-out 129.57   saves 1.70 / 1.20

def priority(item, rem):
    gap = rem - item
    if gap > 21:
        return -gap - 100
    if gap == 3:
        return -gap - 200
    if gap > 24:
        return -gap + 98
    return -gap * 29

Read the table from top to bottom. Every 500-call search beats best fit on the training set by 1.5 to 1.7 bins and on the held-out set by 1.1 to 1.2: a real improvement, about 0.9% fewer bins, and smaller than the training numbers suggest. Give the same seed six times the budget and training improves from 128.70 to 128.20, but the held-out saving moves only from 1.13 to 1.30: the extra calls mostly bought better fits to ten particular instances. The last row makes it vivid. Searching on only two instances produces the biggest training saving of all (2.00 bins) and a held-out saving of 1.33, about a third smaller. The best program on a small training set is the one that happened to suit it. And the hand-written rule from chapter 9, which uses what its author knew about the problem (the smallest item is 20, so a gap of 1 to 19 is dead space), scores 128.40 on the training set and 129.13 on held-out instances, a held-out saving of 1.63 bins, better than any of the searches. The stand-in operator finds improvements; it does not find the insight, and a person who can read the structure of the problem still beats 500 calls of it.

The progress curve in the output has the shape every such search has: fast early gains (130.30 to 129.30 inside 50 calls), then a long tail of small ones. The evolved program in the last lines is not pretty, and it is a good illustration of a point from chapter 9 about reading results: it is best fit (-gap * 29, a steep preference for tight fits) with a heavy penalty for leaving a large gap and for leaving a gap of exactly 3, plus a third rule (gap > 24) that can never fire because the first rule (gap > 21) has already returned. Dead code like that is common in evolved programs and costs nothing but readability. Much of what the search finds is of this kind, a plausible edit of a good rule plus a constant tuned to the training instances.

Try it yourself

Three experiments, each a one-line change to run_demo.py. (1) Compare n_islands=1 with n_islands=4 at 500 calls over six seeds. I measured mean training scores of 128.92 and 128.93 and held-out 129.63 and 129.70: no difference on this small problem, because 500 calls do not give a lineage time to dominate. What would make islands matter? Try a larger budget, a lower cluster_temp, or a fitness landscape with a trap (chapter 3 has the idea). (2) Pass cluster_temp=100 and then cluster_temp=0.05: which end is worse, and why? (3) Remove edit_insert_rule from EDITS and predict the effect before running it; chapter 9's "Try it yourself" asks the same about its dead operator.
